identity.hardware: SAME flight hardware already on orbit (sample carousels, smoke generation duct, 6 L piston aging chamber, diagnostics duct with ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors, P-Trak, DustTrak, ionization chamber, thermal precipitators), with reloaded carousels, 30 loose samples, rebuilt thermal precipitators, and the new MPASS two-angle scattering sensor replacing one Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure

one_line: On the ISS, small pieces of five common spacecraft materials were overheated (without burning) to make smoke, and instruments measured how big the smoke particles were and whether the Shuttle and ISS smoke detectors would have noticed them.
summary: SAME-R, the 2010 reflight of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment, heated small cylindrical samples of Kapton, Teflon, silicone rubber, cotton lampwick and Pyrell foam below ignition in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox. Air flow past the sample was varied from 8.1 cm/s down to zero, sample temperature was set per material, and smoke was aged in a 6 L chamber for up to about 1900 s. Three instruments measured the zeroth, first and third moments of the particle size distribution; a two-angle prototype sensor, Shuttle (ionization) and ISS (light-scattering) detectors and electron-microscope grids recorded the same smoke. Unaged baseline smoke had geometric mean diameters of 0.05-0.18 um and diameters of average mass of 0.11-0.47 um; aging and low flow enlarged the particles, and zero flow gave much larger particles. Kapton and Teflon smoke was smallest and often fell below the ISS detector's alarm level, while silicone, lampwick and Pyrell saturated it. At 8.1 cm/s, flight sizes matched ground tests. The authors conclude that a single-moment detector cannot cover all smokes without nuisance alarms, and that multi-moment detection is promising.

question.text: Spacecraft smoke detectors were designed from terrestrial smoke data, but smoke in orbit may differ. Without buoyancy, smoke stays longer near its source at high concentration, so pyrolysis droplets could grow larger by condensation and coagulation. Spacecraft materials also differ from standard test fuels. The SAME hypothesis was that microgravity liquid smoke would have substantially larger droplets, with fewer particles for the same mass, and that this could stop some detectors from alarming. SAME-R reflew the 2007 SAME experiment to (1) quantify the sizes smoke particles reach in low gravity and relate them to generation temperature, air flow and aging (transport) time; (2) obtain usable electron-microscope (TEM) samples, since all SAME-1 grids came back contaminated; (3) evaluate the existing Shuttle and ISS smoke detectors against these smokes; and (4) demonstrate a prototype two-moment smoke sensor (MPASS). The goal was a database for designing future spacecraft fire detectors and alarm set points.

sources.quote: Unfortunately there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently the fire detectors in current spacecraft were developed based upon terrestrial designs.
The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors.

physics.text: The target is the earliest stage of a spacecraft fire: an overheated material pyrolysing before it ignites, not flaming soot. Heated polymer releases vapour; as the vapour cools, it becomes supersaturated and nucleates particles, which grow by condensation within about a millisecond. Over much longer times (up to about $10^3$ s) particles collide by Brownian motion and coagulate. Liquid particles (lampwick, Kapton, silicone) merge into larger droplets; solid ones (Teflon, Pyrell) stick into fractal-like agglomerates. Coagulation preferentially removes the smallest, most mobile particles, so the count mean diameter grows faster than the diameter of average mass and the size distribution narrows towards a self-preserving geometric standard deviation of about 1.32. In 1 g, a hot plume rises and dilutes the smoke. In microgravity with no forced flow, transport is only by diffusion and thermal expansion (about 4 cm in 60 s), so the smoke stays concentrated, ages faster and forms larger particles. The experiment's 'moment method' measures moments $M_i=\int D^i f_N(D)\,dD$ of the number distribution: $M_0$ (number concentration, condensation particle counter), $M_1$ (roughly the ionization chamber signal) and $M_3$ (roughly the light-scattering mass signal for 0.2-2 um particles). Then $\bar D = M_1/M_0$ and $D_{avm} = (M_3/M_0)^{1/3}$ need no distribution assumption. For a lognormal distribution, $D_p = D_g \exp(p\ln^2\sigma_g)$ with $p=0.5$ and $1.5$ for these two diameters, so $D_g$ and $\sigma_g$ follow from their ratio. Detector physics matters: an ionization detector responds roughly to $M_1$ and favours numerous small particles, while a forward-scattering detector responds strongly to particles near or above its near-IR wavelength (about 1 um) and weakly to particles of about 0.1 um.

equations.meaning: Brownian coagulation of an aerosol with number concentration $N$ (cm$^{-3}$) and an effective coagulation coefficient $K$ (cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$, of order $10^{-9}$ for 0.1-1 um particles in air). Explains why concentrated smoke (a few $10^6$ cm$^{-3}$) aged in the 6 L chamber lost a factor of 1.7-2.7 in number over about 800 s while $D_{avm}$ grew. It also explains why concentrations below about $10^6$ cm$^{-3}$ (the drum tests, < $2\times10^4$ cm$^{-3}$) age negligibly. The monodisperse constant-K form is approximate for polydisperse smoke.

equations.meaning: Investigators' estimate for zero flow in microgravity. Pyrolysis gases spread only by diffusion (effective diffusivity $\mathcal{D}$, cm$^2$/s) over a length $\ell$ in time $t$. In 60 s they fill about 64 cm$^3$ instead of being diluted into the 6000 cm$^3$ aging chamber, so the initial smoke concentration is of order 50 times higher (their figure), and coagulation is correspondingly faster. This is an order-of-magnitude scaling. The 2018 paper instead estimates the vapour concentration as about 8 times higher, from a thermal-expansion flow of 0.5-1.5 cm/s.

sources.quote: If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case.

The vapor concentration is inversely proportional to the flow so the nominal vapor concentration for the zero-flow case is about eight times higher than for the standard 8.1 cm/s forced flow condition.

apparatus.text: The SAME hardware was installed in the MSG. A sample carousel (six positions) indexed each sample into the smoke generation duct. A stainless-steel wire coiled around the sample both heated it and sensed its temperature through its resistance. A feedback loop held the wire at a set resistance ratio Rt/R0 for about 60 s. A rising piston in a 6 L (6000 cm3) aging chamber drew air past the sample, setting the duct velocity, and captured the smoke. Some smoke was pushed almost immediately into a low-volume diagnostics duct ('unaged'); the rest was held for a set time (secondary aging) and then measured. The diagnostics duct held: the ISS smoke detector (2-pass near-IR laser-diode forward scattering at 30 degrees, minimum reported sensitivity 0.3 um, planned alarm level 2 V); the Space Shuttle (STS) detector (dual-chamber ionization with a pump and inertial separator that rejects particles larger than 1-2 um); a modified TSI P-Trak condensation particle counter for $M_0$, fed through a dynamic nitrogen diluter; a First Alert residential ionization chamber (americium-241) calibrated for $M_1$; and a TSI DustTrak 90-degree photometer for $M_3$ (calibrated per material against a tapered-element oscillating microbalance). For SAME-R, one of the two DustTrak enclosures was replaced by the GRC-built MPASS, which detects scattered light at two angles to estimate the 2nd and 3rd moments. Thermal precipitators (a heated wire above a TEM grid, so particles deposit by thermophoresis) sampled smoke before and after aging for post-flight TEM. The six rebuilt precipitators held 12 grids each.

procedure.text: Six carousels were preloaded (one Pyrell sample in carousel 5 was found unusable, probably shaken loose at launch). Thirty loose samples (6 Pyrell, 6 silicone, 9 Kapton, 5 lampwick, 4 Teflon) were later loaded into carousel 4 in groups, logged as carousels 7(4)-11(4). For each run, the operator set the wire resistance ratio Rt/R0 (material-specific: about 1.22-1.23 for Pyrell, 1.245-1.28 for lampwick, 1.30-1.36 for silicone, 1.38-1.48 for Kapton, 1.445-1.452 for Teflon). The sample was heated for 60 s (one Kapton run 120 s) while the piston drew air through the duct at 8.1 cm/s (baseline), 2 or 1 cm/s, or zero. Zero flow was not in the original design; it was obtained by changing the valve sequence. The baseline temperature was chosen to give 1-2 mg of mass loss in 60 s. Smoke was usually given 11 s of primary aging and 8 s of mixing, then half was measured unaged (net aging about 21-62 s). The rest was aged in the chamber and measured at about 218-1923 s ('a' runs in the table). Five 'aged STS det' runs held all the smoke for 720 s before measurement. The STS detector was used only in selected runs because its pump drew too much flow to allow aging. Flights ran from 16 July to 9 September 2010 in seven periods, with the science team at GRC's Telescience Center. Samples were weighed before and after flight for mass loss. Afterwards, three ground campaigns ran: (a) flow tests to correct the instruments' dilution ratios; (b) 1 g TEM tests under flight conditions; and (c) 'smoke-in-drums' tests in which smoke from the identical ground SAME unit was diluted into 55-gallon drums and measured with a TSI 3936 scanning mobility particle sizer (SMPS) to test the lognormal assumption. Actual wire (sample) temperatures were later derived from the logged resistances with a two-section wire heat-balance model.

psi_data.summary: PSI-101 holds 343 files (about 6.3 GB). The most useful file is the analysed workbook 'SAME, SAME-R_Results.xlsx' (about 45 sheets). It holds per-run reduced data for SAME-1, SAME-R and ground tests: test conditions, ISS and STS detector voltages, P-Trak, DustTrak and MPASS outputs, moment diameters, Hatch-Choate sigma_g and D_g, sample temperature and mass loss. It also has sheets for detector-alarm analysis, flight vs ground and SMPS drum comparisons. Another 70 or so per-run .xls files hold the reduced time series for runs 48-114, and per-run TEM size-analysis workbooks cover runs 54, 55, 60, 62, 63, 64 and 94. The 89-page final report (2014) includes the test matrix (Appendix A), mass loss (Appendix C), the TEM grid map (Appendix D/E) and the 2012 ICES paper (Appendix F). Raw data (223 files, 5.7 GB) are mostly not downloaded: 78 zips (1.7 GB), 8 MP4 downlink videos (3.7 GB), 44 housekeeping CSVs and 74 TEM image decks (pptx). The engineering documents are SAME-era (EIRD, verification plan, wire tests). The two legacy .ppt presentations could not be read. The experimental table CSV is a 10-column extract of Appendix A.

findings.claim: Unaged baseline smoke at 8 cm/s was sub-micrometre for every material. Kapton had geometric mean diameter Dg = 0.047 um, count mean 0.062 um and diameter of average mass 0.106 um. Teflon had Dg 0.093 um and D_avm 0.173 um, lampwick 0.103 and 0.271 um, silicone 0.152 and 0.468 um, and Pyrell 0.177 and 0.377 um. The geometric standard deviation was 2.03-2.38. Typical runs had a few million particles per cm3 and 2-15 mg/m3. (These are the final-report values; the appended 2012 paper gives slightly different numbers, e.g. Kapton Dg 0.042 um.)

sources.quote: For typical runs, the partic le concentrations were a few million particles / cc and the mass concentrations were 2 to 15 mg/m 3 however there were runs with fewer particles.

findings.claim: Aging the smoke for 720 s in the chamber made the particles larger and the distribution narrower. D_avm rose from 0.106 to 0.169 um (Kapton), 0.271 to 0.401 um (lampwick), 0.468 to 0.628 um (silicone) and 0.377 to 0.529 um (Pyrell), and sigma_g fell to 1.67-1.96. Teflon was the exception: Dg did not grow (0.093 to 0.080 um) and sigma_g widened to 2.34. Number counts fell by a factor of 1.7-2.7 over about 800 s. This agreed with coagulation theory within about 20% for number and 4% for D_avm, but sigma_g fell more than twice as much as predicted.

findings.claim: Lower air flow past the overheated sample produced larger particles for Kapton, Teflon and lampwick (runs from 8.1 down to 2 cm/s). The authors infer that smoke trapped in a poorly ventilated avionics enclosure will be substantially larger than smoke released into ventilated cabin air. The 2018 analysis puts the possible increase in D_avm at low flow at up to a factor of 2.5.

sources.quote: These figures show a strong trend of increased particle size at low flow ra tes. This indicates that sm oke trapped in an avionics enclosure can be expected to be substantially larger than smoke released in ventilated areas.
The potential error of this analogy can be estimated using Figure 6 which suggests that lower flow rates could increase the diameter of average mass by as much as a factor of 2.5.

findings.claim: In the 11 zero-flow runs (smoke moved only by diffusion and thermal expansion, at about 0.5-1.5 cm/s seen on video), D_avm was larger than at 8.1 cm/s. The sources quantify this differently: 30-40% larger for all materials (final report text); 2-3 times larger (conclusions of the appended 2012 paper); and on average a factor of 1.7, ranging from 1.3 for Teflon to 2.8 for Kapton (2018 journal paper). Example: silicone run 104 at 0 cm/s had D_avm 1.22 um vs 0.42-0.47 um in the 8.1 cm/s baseline runs.

sources.quote: It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests.
The zero flow conditions produced smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate.

The diameter of average mass is a factor of 1.7 larger for the zero-flow compared to the standard flow condition. This is an average for all the materials, which vary from as low as 1.3 for Teflon to 2.8 for Kapton.

The thermal expansion induced smoke-flow observed with a video camera ranged from 0.5 cm/s to 1.5 cm/s with the higher velocity corresponding to Kapton and Teflon with the highest pyrolysis temperatures.

findings.claim: The prototype two-moment sensor MPASS was tested with a single least-squares third-order correlation fitted to all test points with signal-to-noise > 2, regardless of material, heating rate or aging. The correlation cut the relative variance of the size-normalised response by at least a factor of 2 compared with a single-output sensor. Mass-concentration prediction was better than number prediction, consistent with MPASS having been optimised for mass. The authors conclude that a two-moment sensor can tell a high smoke concentration from a lower concentration of large dust particles.

The resulting variance for the mass response is substantially lower than for the number concentration.

The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, a feature which can minimize false smoke detector alarms.

findings.claim: Clean TEM grids were recovered this time (70-72 grid samples, compared with all SAME-1 grids being contaminated). They show distinct morphologies by material. Kapton and lampwick formed spherical droplets; Kapton particles were small and rarely agglomerated, and lampwick particles were 200-1400 nm. Teflon formed agglomerates of uniform primaries under about 200 nm, while Pyrell formed agglomerates of primaries widely spread in size. Silicone left no TEM-visible particles, presumably because liquid droplets evaporated in the vacuum. The visible effect of aging was the disappearance of the smallest particles, not a growth of the large ones.

findings.claim: The ground SMPS drum tests checked the lognormal assumption behind the moment method. Kapton and lampwick smoke were well described by lognormal distributions. Silicone was not: it had a shoulder at small sizes and a steeper large-size tail, and the SMPS (up to 1000 nm) captured only about 40% of its volume distribution. Teflon and Pyrell aggregates are non-spherical and were excluded. In flight, TEM and moment-method diameters agreed well for Kapton, the best-suited smoke. For lampwick, Kapton and Pyrell, the moment method gave a reasonable D_avm.

relevance.text: SAME-R is the main PSI dataset on what early (pre-flaming) spacecraft smoke looks like to a detector. Overheated Kapton and Teflon, the insulation materials most likely to overheat first in electrical faults, give very small particles (D_avm about 0.1-0.2 um unaged). The ISS forward-scattering detector would often not alarm on these. Silicone, cellulose and Pyrell give large particles that saturate it. The older Shuttle ionization design handles small particles better but rejects particles above 1-2 um, and long aging or stagnant (avionics-box) conditions push smoke towards those sizes. The authors conclude that a single-moment detector cannot be sensitive across this size range and also reject large background dust. They recommend size-selective detection, either by classifying particles or by measuring two or more moments, as the MPASS demonstrated, possibly with gas-species sensing. Because 1 g and microgravity smoke matched at 8.1 cm/s, ground tests with controlled aging can screen detectors for ventilated conditions. Low-flow and stagnant microgravity cases still need special attention, because they produce larger, differently shaped particles.

sources.quote: However, this is a concern as Kapton and Teflon are very commonly used in spacecraft, especially in electrical systems where they can be expected to be among the first materials to overheat in a smoke-producing event.

habitat_conditions.text: All smoke was generated in MSG air, and the documents do not report oxygen fraction or pressure (presumably ISS cabin air near sea-level conditions: about 20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa). No tests were made in the enriched-oxygen, reduced-pressure atmospheres planned for exploration (e.g. 30% or more O2 at 70.3 kPa or less for a lunar habitat). Pyrolysis rates and particle formation could differ there, and the lower gas density changes diffusion and coagulation rates. The results also cover only 0-8.1 cm/s local flow and pre-ignition heating, not flaming soot.

earth_benefits.text: The investigators note that smoke detectors developed from SAME results could serve other confined, hard-to-evacuate environments such as submarines and underwater laboratories. The moment-method and two-moment sensing approach also bears on reducing nuisance alarms in terrestrial detectors.

limitations.text: Instrument uncertainties are large: about +/-30% for the zeroth moment, +/-12% for the first and +/-25% for the third. Diameter repeatability is about +/-15%. Many smokes exceeded the calibration range of the ionization (first-moment) chamber, which most affects Dg and sigma_g.

gaps: The two legacy .ppt presentations ('Measurement of Smoke Particle Size under Low-Gravity Conditions', 'Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires') have no extracted text and were not read.

The detector-performance figures (alarm boundaries in Fig. 9 of the 2018 paper; slides 23-26 of the 2013 talk) are images only. Alarm counts were taken from the 2018 paper text and recomputed from raw ISS volts against the 2 V planned alarm level, without offset correction. The STS alarm threshold voltage was not found in the documents read.
Oxygen fraction, pressure and humidity in the MSG during tests are not stated in the documents read (final report, presentations, EIRD excerpts, BCDD).

Table 1 (baseline diameters) appears with two different value sets in the same final report (pp. 4-5 vs Appendix F p. 78, e.g. Kapton unaged Dg 0.047 vs 0.042 um). This record quotes the main-text set.

The size increase at zero flow is reported inconsistently: 30-40% (final report text), 2-3x (appended 2012 paper conclusions), factor 1.7 average (2018 paper). Smoke lost at zero flow is 'about half' vs 'about 2/3'.
TEM sample count is 70 (final report, flight operation section) vs 72 (results section and 2018 paper).

Run counts differ: the PSI record says 66 test points, the final report 67 runs (109 entries including secondary aging). The experimental-table CSV has 109 rows, but one is a mislabelled duplicate ('Teflon, 57', Rt/R0 1.253, which Appendix A lists as lampwick reburn run 57), and Kapton run 112 (2 cm/s, STS) is missing.
The PSI record's experimentHardware field says 'Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware' with a 1996 NTRS link. That describes the earlier CSD experiment, not the SAME hardware actually used.
The SAME Operations Manual contains laptop FTP instructions with an internal IP address and anonymous login. They were not copied; no real credentials were seen.
Sample dimensions (about 0.5 cm x 1.3 cm) come only from the 2018 journal paper; the PSI documents read do not state them.
Most raw data (zips, MP4 downlink video, housekeeping CSVs) are not downloaded and were not inspected.
